 Here’s What the Average 62-Year-Old American Could Receive in Social Security in 2027
 Chris Lewis, CEPF 2026년 11월 21일 토 오전 10:00 UTC 0 
 Turning 62 is a milestone a lot of Americans watch for, since it's the earliest
 age you can claim Social Security retirement benefits. But claiming at 62 also
 comes with a trade-off that can follow you for the rest of your life: a
 permanently reduced monthly check compared with claiming at full retirement age.
 With the Social Security Administration's 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA)
 now confirmed for 2027, many people want to know what that adjustment actually
 means for a typical check. The answer involves a little math, a few important
 caveats, and a reminder that "average" doesn't mean "yours."
 Understanding what Social Security could pay is one step toward avoiding
 common financial
 mistakes in retirement.
 Find Out: 13 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about. 
 How we got this estimate
 The Social Security Administration's latest age-specific data show an average
 monthly benefit of $1,424.40 for retired-worker beneficiaries age 62 as of
 December 2025. That amount already includes the 2.8% COLA for 2026: the increase
 applied to December benefits, which were paid in January. We therefore don't
 apply that increase again.
 On Oct. 14, 2026, SSA announced a 3.6% COLA for 2027, reflected in payments
 starting in January 2027. Applying that increase to $1,424.40 gives
 approximately $1,475.68 a month before deductions, or about $17,708 for 12
 months of benefits.
 This is a COLA-adjusted illustration, not an observed 2027 average or a
 guaranteed starting payment. Individual benefits — and the actual 2027
 average — will depend on recipients' earnings histories and claiming decisions.

 Why 62-year-olds typically get smaller checks than the overall average
 SSA estimates that all retired workers will receive an average monthly benefit
 of $2,170 in January 2027. People who claim at 62 tend to receive less than that
 broader average, in part because claiming before full retirement age (FRA)
 permanently reduces their monthly benefit.
 SSA's age-reduction chart shows how much that reduction can be. For anyone born
 in 1960 or later, FRA is 67, and claiming at 62 means taking benefits a full 60
 months early. That triggers a 30% reduction from what the same person would
 receive by waiting until FRA, according to SSA. The reduction formula is 5/9 of
 1% for each of the first 36 months claimed early, plus 5/12 of 1% for each
 additional month beyond that, per SSA's benefit calculation rules.
 To put that in dollar terms using SSA's own 2026 examples: workers who earned at
 or above the taxable maximum every year starting at age 22 and began receiving
 benefits in 2026 could receive $4,152 a month at full retirement age, $2,969 at
 62, or $5,181 at 70. These examples describe workers of different ages starting
 benefits in the same year, rather than three choices for the same person. The
 $5,181 figure is not a universal maximum for everyone receiving retirement
 benefits.
 Most people don't have 35 years of maximum taxable earnings, so their numbers
 will fall well below these high-earner examples. But the pattern holds at every
 income level: claiming at 62 locks in a lower monthly payment for life compared
 with waiting, aside from the benefit recalculations SSA performs if you keep
 working.
 What actually determines your personal check
 Your benefit is based on your own 35 highest years of wage-indexed earnings,
 which SSA uses to calculate your Average Indexed Monthly Earnings (AIME). That
 AIME feeds into a formula that produces your Primary Insurance Amount (PIA), the
 benefit you'd receive starting exactly at FRA. Claim earlier than FRA, and SSA
 applies a reduction; delay claiming beyond FRA, up to age 70, and SSA applies an
 increase.

 Years in the workforce
 If you have fewer than 35 years of earnings, SSA counts zeros for the missing
 years, which can meaningfully lower your average.
 Earnings level
 Higher lifetime earnings, up to the taxable maximum each year ($184,500 in 2026,
 rising to $192,300 in 2027, according to SSA), generally produce a higher
 benefit.
 Spousal or survivor status
 Benefits based on a spouse's or deceased spouse's earnings record follow
 different rules and percentages.

 Continued work after claiming
 SSA automatically recalculates your benefit if a later year of earnings turns
 out to be one of your highest 35, potentially increasing your check even after
 you've started collecting.
 Gross benefit versus what actually lands in your account
 The dollar figures above, like the $1,475.68 illustration or SSA's claiming-age
 examples, are gross monthly benefits before any deductions. What actually gets
 deposited can be noticeably lower.
 The most common deduction is the Medicare Part B premium, which is typically
 withheld directly from Social Security checks. The standard Part B premium is
 $202.90 a month in 2026, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid
 Services (CMS), and higher earners pay more under Medicare's income-related
 monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA) rules. Some beneficiaries also have federal
 tax withholding, Medicare Part D premiums, or garnishments for debts like unpaid
 federal taxes deducted from their gross benefit.
 Beneficiaries can review their own gross benefit, deductions, and net deposit
 amount by creating or checking their "my Social Security" account at ssa.gov.
 Bottom line
 Applying the 2027 COLA to SSA's December 2025 age-62 average gives approximately
 $1,475.68 a month, or $17,708 for 12 months, before deductions. This is a
 COLA-adjusted illustration, not an observed 2027 average or a guaranteed
 starting payment. Your own benefit depends on your earnings history and when you
 claim.
 The most reliable way to know what you can expect is to check your own numbers.
 SSA's online Social Security Statement, available through a free "my Social
 Security" account, shows personalized estimates at different claiming ages based
 on your actual earnings record, which is a far more useful planning tool than
 any national average.

 if you're living on just Social Security .
